title_en: Wu Xiaoqin v. Shaanxi Broadcast & TV Network Media Co., Ltd. — dispute over tied transaction
ruling_gist_en: The basic digital TV subscription and maintenance fee and the digital TV pay-program fee are two separate services. An operator providing digital TV services, by leveraging its dominant market position, charges both the basic digital TV subscription and maintenance fee and the digital TV pay-program fee together, which objectively affects consumers' ability to choose other service providers for related digital pay programs, and also hinders other service providers from entering this television service market, resulting in adverse effects on market competition. This violates the provisions of Article 17, Paragraph 1, Item 5 of the Anti-Monopoly Law.

full_text_en:
Wu Xiaoqin v. Shaanxi Broadcast and TV Network Media Co., Ltd.
— dispute over bundled transaction

Ruling Summary

The basic digital TV viewing maintenance fee and the digital TV pay-program fee are two separate services. An operator providing digital TV services that, by exploiting its dominant market position, collects both fees together objectively affects consumers' ability to choose other service providers for related digital pay programs, and also hinders other service providers from entering this TV service market, producing an adverse effect on market competition, in violation of Article 17(1)(v) of the Anti-Monopoly Law.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court
(2016) Supreme People's Court Civil Retrial No. 98

Retrial Applicant (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): Wu Xiaoqin, male, born January 12, 1969, Han Chinese, employee of Weicheng Branch of Xianyang City Administration for Industry and Commerce, residing at Room 103, South Unit, 128 Yifeng West Street, Xianyang City, Shaanxi Province.

Agent ad litem: Guo Hui, lawyer at Shaanxi Wugong Law Firm.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Shaanxi Broadcast and TV Network Media (Group) Co., Ltd. Domicile: No. 15 Gaoxin 1st Road, Xi'an, Shaanxi Province.

Legal Representative: Lü Xiaoming, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Lu Ziwen, lawyer at Shaanxi Haipu Ruicheng Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Huang Shiling, lawyer at Shaanxi Haipu Ruicheng Law Firm.

Retrial Applicant Wu Xiaoqin, in the case of dispute over bundled transaction with Respondent Shaanxi Broadcast and TV Network Media (Group) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "Guangdian Network"), dissatisfied with the Civil Judgment (2013) Shaan Min San Zhong Zi No. 38 of the Shaanxi High People's Court, applied to this Court for retrial. After trial, this Court issued on September 7, 2015 the Civil Ruling (2014) Min Shen Zi No. 278 to grant retrial of this case. After the retrial was granted, this Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law and heard this case through a public session held on April 7, 2016. Retrial Applicant Wu Xiaoqin and his agent ad litem Guo Hui, and the agent ad litem of Respondent Guangdian Network, Lu Ziwen, appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. The review of this case is now concluded.

Wu Xiaoqin applied for retrial on the grounds that:

(1) The application of law in the second-instance judgment is erroneous. 1. When selling the products to Wu Xiaoqin, Guangdian Network did not inform him that the basic viewing program and the value-added pay program are two separate products that can be purchased separately, and then sold the two products together to Wu Xiaoqin, which constitutes a tying arrangement regulated by the Anti-Monopoly Law. The second-instance judgment held that "in this case, Guangdian Network did not adopt a method of not selling separately when selling; it provided not only bundled services but also basic services, giving consumers more than two choices. In particular, the basic viewing maintenance fee is subject to government pricing, and in fact, there were transactions for separate purchases during the same period, meaning that consumers could choose not to purchase the bundled products; the right to choose existed. Since the right to choose existed, it does not meet the constituent elements of a tying arrangement" – this constitutes an error in the application of law. 2. In this case, there was no situation of inability to provide evidence or insufficient evidence. The second-instance judgment's application of the "Several Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Litigation" does not conform to the legislative intent of that provision and constitutes an error in the application of law.

(2) The composition of the trial organization in the second-instance procedure was unlawful. In the second-instance procedure, the judge who issued the summons to Wu Xiaoqin was Feng Ju; the members of the collegial panel at the trial hearing were Tong Huihui, Feng Ju, and Chang Baotang. However, the collegial panel members signed on the second-instance judgment were Tong Huihui, Song Xiaomin, and Chang Baotang. This situation of "the informed collegial panel members, after the trial has been held, but the signatures on the legal document are different" falls under the "unlawful composition of the trial organization" as provided in Article 200(1)(vii) of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC. The second-instance judgment erred in applying the law and the composition of the trial organization was unlawful. Therefore, he requests that the second-instance judgment be reversed and the first-instance judgment be affirmed.

Guangdian Network submitted its defense opinion stating:

(1) The second-instance court correctly applied the law. 1. From both the facts and the application of law, this case has no relation to any monopoly conduct. Wu Xiaoqin alleged in the first instance that the dispute arose because Guangdian Network infringed his "right to free choice", leading to the fact that he was forced to pay the viewing fee of 15 yuan. According to Article 9 of the Law of the PRC on the Protection of Consumer Rights and Interests (hereinafter referred to as the Consumer Rights Protection Law), the "right to free choice" means that consumers have the right to freely choose goods or services. Therefore, this case is a dispute over whether the rights that Wu Xiaoqin is entitled to under the Consumer Rights Protection Law were infringed, and has nothing to do with monopoly conduct. 2. Wu Xiaoqin's claim that Guangdian Network's concealment of the truth combined with its dominant market position constitutes a tying arrangement regulated by the Anti-Monopoly Law is illogical. Guangdian Network did not conceal the truth; the composition of the charges was clearly informed to Wu Xiaoqin at the time of consumption. Guangdian Network never forced Wu Xiaoqin to consume; Guangdian Network's sales conduct is normal sales conduct and does not constitute a tying arrangement. In addition, to ascertain the truth, Guangdian Network submitted to the court during the second instance receipts for the same period showing that Guangdian Network collected only the basic viewing fee on a monthly basis; this situation was not an isolated case, and the second-instance court has already found this as a fact. Wu Xiaoqin's subjective speculation that these individuals were all friends and acquaintances of our company has no factual basis or supporting evidence.

(2) The composition of the trial organization in the second-instance procedure was lawful and valid. The second-instance procedure was lawful and valid, and the members of the collegial panel participated in the entire trial proceedings in accordance with the law. It requests this Court to reject Wu Xiaoqin's retrial application and uphold the second-instance judgment.

This case was originally filed by Wu Xiaoqin with the Xi'an Intermediate People's Court of Shaanxi Province. Wu Xiaoqin alleged to that court: He is a digital TV user of Guangdian Network. On May 10, 2012, when he went to pay the basic digital TV viewing maintenance fee to Guangdian Network, a staff member of Guangdian Network informed him that the monthly minimum fee had been raised from 25 yuan to 30 yuan starting from March 2012, and that the minimum payment at a time was for one quarter. After Wu Xiaoqin paid the viewing fee for the period from May 10, 2012 to August 9, 2012 according to the above rate, he found that the fee items and amounts on the invoice were: basic digital TV viewing maintenance fee 75 yuan and digital TV program fee 15 yuan. Upon inquiry, he learned that the reason for the increase was a system upgrade, and after the upgrade, several programs would be added for users. Wu Xiaoqin then called Guangdian Network's customer service hotline and received the same response. Wu Xiaoqin checked the "Notice on the Standard for Basic Digital TV Viewing Maintenance Fees in the Whole Province" issued by the Shaanxi Provincial Price Bureau and learned that the basic digital TV viewing maintenance fee for urban residents in cities and above county level in Shaanxi Province is 25 yuan per main terminal per month; cable digital TV users may voluntarily choose to pay the basic viewing maintenance fee monthly, quarterly, or annually according to the actual situation. After paying the basic digital TV viewing maintenance fee, users may receive the following services provided by Guangdian Network: (1) no fewer than 58 channels of standard-definition digital TV programs; (2) digital audio broadcasting services (20 channels); (3) electronic program guide service; (4) automatic channel list update service; (5) information service, including government information (government reports, government affairs updates, government procurement, policy information of the province, cities, counties, and various functional departments) and life information (weather forecasts, news, traffic, tourism, real estate, public announcements, medical care, etc.). Wu Xiaoqin believes that Guangdian Network's collection of 15 yuan as digital TV program fee from Wu Xiaoqin was in fact for providing additional service content beyond the scope of the above services; with respect to this, Wu Xiaoqin should have the right to freely choose. Guangdian Network is a public utility enterprise or other business unit that is legally in a monopolistic position, and has a dominant position in the digital TV market. The above conduct of Guangdian Network violates Article 17(1)(v) of the Anti-Monopoly Law of the PRC (hereinafter referred to as the Anti-Monopoly Law), which prohibits "a business operator with a dominant market position from, without justifiable reasons, tying goods or imposing other unreasonable trading conditions in transactions", infringing upon his lawful rights and interests. Therefore, he filed a lawsuit with the court, requesting: (1) that the collection of 15 yuan digital TV program fee from Wu Xiaoqin on May 10, 2012 by Guangdian Network be declared invalid; (2) that Guangdian Network refund 15 yuan to Wu Xiaoqin; (3) that the litigation costs be borne by the defendant.

Guangdian Network argued in the first instance: First, Guangdian Network has the responsibility to provide more TV programs to users. Guangdian Network is the only operator lawfully engaged in cable TV transmission business and the only centralized broadcaster of TV programs in Shaanxi Province, approved by the Shaanxi Provincial Government. To meet the diverse needs of the vast number of users for TV programs, it has the responsibility and obligation to provide increasingly rich and colorful TV programs beyond the basic viewing programs according to market demand; this fully serves the interests of the vast majority of the people. Since most distinctive TV programs are purchased and introduced, Guangdian Network, in order to meet the diverse consumption needs of users and expand its business scale, charges additional fees to consumers who choose to watch programs beyond the basic viewing program; this conforms to the Anti-Monopoly Law's provisions encouraging state-owned enterprises to expand business scale and enhance market competitiveness, and has received positive recognition and support from governments at all levels. Second, Guangdian Network did not abuse its dominant market position. Guangdian Network has a dominant position in the cable TV market in Shaanxi Province and encourages users to choose richer cable TV packages, but it has not abused its dominant market position, nor has it forced users to consume services beyond the basic viewing service. Among Guangdian Network's current 4.5 million users, most choose diverse and personalized cable packages higher than the basic viewing fee, and are willing to purchase richer TV programs beyond the state-approved basic viewing programs to meet their own spiritual and cultural needs; however, Guangdian Network also has a large number of users who only watch basic programs. The vast majority of users have full freedom of choice. Third, Wu Xiaoqin does not have the right to request that the monopoly conduct be declared invalid. The determination and punishment of monopoly conduct belongs to administrative power, not judicial power. Wu Xiaoqin has the right to file a lawsuit for civil damages due to harm caused by monopoly conduct, but does not have the right to directly request the people's court to confirm in an administrative lawsuit whether monopoly conduct is established. Wu Xiaoqin's first request for relief has no legal basis. Finally, Guangdian Network's lawful business activities should be protected. To ensure national information security, the Party and the government exercise strict supervision over the propaganda industry, forming a state-controlled position in cable TV business, implementing provincial monopoly, and carrying out supervision and regulation in accordance with the law. At the same time, the Party and the government also require cable TV operators to add programs and charge fees beyond the basic viewing programs under conditions consistent with economic laws, in order to meet the growing cultural needs of the broad masses; conversely, if they cannot charge fees beyond the basic viewing programs, the normal maintenance and upgrading of the network will be disrupted, and the diverse choices of users at different levels cannot be satisfied, which essentially indirectly harms the right of the vast majority of the people to choose to watch more TV programs. Therefore, although Guangdian Network has launched a series of TV packages to meet users' personalized choices, it has never engaged in forced tying; it operates in accordance with the law, ensuring the right of the vast majority of the people to choose to watch more TV programs. Therefore, it requests that Wu Xiaoqin's request to declare invalid the addition of programs and collection of fees by Guangdian Network be rejected; and it expresses willingness to actively resolve Wu Xiaoqin's second request for relief.

The first-instance court found through trial the following facts: On May 10, 2012, Wu Xiaoqin went to Guangdian Network to pay the basic digital TV viewing maintenance fee. Guangdian Network informed Wu Xiaoqin that the monthly minimum basic digital TV viewing maintenance fee had been raised from 25 yuan to 30 yuan starting from March 2012, and that the minimum payment at a time was for one quarter. Wu Xiaoqin then paid 90 yuan as the basic digital TV viewing maintenance fee for the period from May 10, 2012 to August 9, 2012 as required by Guangdian Network. Guangdian Network issued a special fee invoice to Wu Xiaoqin. The invoice stated: customer name: Wu Xiaoqin; address: Room 4-602, Building 3, Mingshi Yaju, Timber Company, Dongfeng Road, Xianyang City; user code: c10002389556; fee items: basic digital TV viewing maintenance fee 75 yuan and digital TV program fee 15 yuan, totaling 90 yuan; fee period: May 10, 2012 to August 9, 2012. Thereafter, Wu Xiaoqin consulted through Guangdian Network's customer service center (service hotline: 96766) and learned that Guangdian Network had upgraded its programs, adding different pay programs with different packages. Among them, the basic viewing fee for the lowest package was 360 yuan per year, or 30 yuan per month, and users had to pay for at least three months each time.

It was also found that: On December 2, 2004, the National Development and Reform Commission and the State Administration of Radio, Film and Television issued the "Interim Measures for Management of Basic Cable TV Viewing Maintenance Fees" (Fa Gai Jia Ge [2004] No. 2787). The Measures provide that basic cable TV viewing maintenance fees are subject to government pricing, and the fee rates are determined by the price authorities; the Measures also provide for the nature, determination, and principles and basis for setting or adjusting the basic cable TV viewing maintenance fee rates. On July 11, 2005, the State Administration of Radio, Film and Television issued the "Several Opinions on Promoting the Overall Digital Conversion of Cable TV in Pilot Units (Trial)", in which item 3 provides: "In the process of promoting overall conversion, each pilot unit shall pay attention to the promotion of new services such as pay channels, video on demand, interactive TV, and high-definition TV, for users to freely choose and voluntarily subscribe." On May 29, 2006, the Shaanxi Provincial Price Bureau issued the "Notice on the Standard for Basic Digital TV Viewing Maintenance Fees in the Whole Province" (Shan Jia Jing Fa [2006] No. 84), which stipulates: The standard for basic digital TV viewing maintenance fee is: the billing unit is one receiving terminal per TV set watched by a resident user. For urban resident users in cities and above county level in the province, the fee is 25 yuan per main terminal per month; cable digital TV users may voluntarily choose to pay the basic viewing maintenance fee monthly, quarterly, or annually according to the actual situation. Cable digital TV network operators shall not force users to pay the annual fee in one lump sum. The basic viewing service in Shaanxi Province's cable digital TV shall include no fewer than 58 channels of standard-definition digital TV programs. On August 25, 2009, the National Development and Reform Commission and the State Administration of Radio, Film and Television issued the "Notice on Strengthening Cable TV Fee Management and Related Issues" (Fa Gai Jia Ge [2009] No. 2201), which states: Basic cable TV viewing maintenance fees are subject to government pricing; fees for cable TV value-added services and digital TV pay programs are to be determined by the cable TV operating entities themselves.

It was further found that: Guangdian Network is the only operator lawfully engaged in cable TV transmission business and the only centralized broadcaster of TV programs in Shaanxi Province, approved by the Shaanxi Provincial Government. Guangdian Network admitted that it occupies a dominant position in the cable TV transmission business in Shaanxi Province.

The first-instance court, after trial, held that the main issues of dispute in this case are: (1) Whether Guangdian Network engaged in tying or imposing other unreasonable trading conditions prohibited by the Anti-Monopoly Law; (2) Whether Guangdian Network's collection of digital TV pay-program fees from Wu Xiaoqin is valid.

(1) Regarding whether Guangdian Network engaged in tying or imposing other unreasonable trading conditions prohibited by the Anti-Monopoly Law.

A tying arrangement refers to the conduct of a business operator who, in the process of providing goods or services in a transaction, exploits its dominant market position to, contrary to the purchaser's will, sell together or provide another kind of goods or service that the purchaser does not need. The conduct of imposing unreasonable conditions refers to the conduct of a business operator who, in the process of providing goods or services, contrary to the purchaser's will, forcibly imposes other unreasonable conditions and requires the purchaser to accept them, and the purchaser has to accept such unreasonable conditions because of the business operator's dominant market position.

Article 17(1) of the Anti-Monopoly Law provides: Business operators with a dominant market position are prohibited from engaging in the following acts of abusing their dominant market position: ... (5) tying goods or imposing other unreasonable trading conditions in transactions without justifiable reasons. This provision indicates that the following conditions must be met to constitute a tying arrangement prohibited by the Anti-Monopoly Law: the business operator has a dominant position in the relevant market; the business operator exploits its dominant position in the relevant market to engage in tying or impose other unreasonable trading conditions in transactions; and the business operator lacks justifiable reasons for tying goods or imposing other unreasonable trading conditions in transactions. In this case, whether Guangdian Network's provision of digital TV services meets the constituent elements of the above-mentioned tying or imposition of unreasonable trading conditions is the key to whether Wu Xiaoqin's grounds for litigation can be established.

First, the definition of the relevant market in this case. The definition of the relevant market is the starting point of anti-monopoly litigation cases. Only by defining the relevant market can it be further determined whether a dominant market position exists and whether the disputed conduct constitutes a monopoly. Article 12(2) of the Anti-Monopoly Law provides: For the purposes of this Law, "relevant market" means the scope of goods and the territorial scope within which business operators compete with respect to specific goods or services (hereinafter collectively referred to as "goods") during a certain period. This indicates that two core elements, the product and the territory, must be considered in determining the relevant market. According to the facts found in this case, the relevant service market involved in the alleged monopoly conduct is the cable TV transmission service market, and the territorial scope of this relevant service market is the Shaanxi Province region.

Second, whether Guangdian Network has a dominant position in the relevant market. Article 17(2) of the Anti-Monopoly Law provides: For the purposes of this Law, "dominant market position" means a market position held by a business operator that enables it to control the price, quantity, or other trading conditions of goods, or to obstruct or affect the ability of other business operators to enter the relevant market. According to the facts found in this case, the conduct alleged by Wu Xiaoqin is that Guangdian Network, by exploiting its dominant position in the cable TV transmission service market within Shaanxi Province, forcibly tied the additional service content when providing basic digital TV viewing services. Since the cable TV transmission service market is subject to provincial monopoly, and Guangdian Network is the only operator lawfully engaged in cable TV transmission business and the only centralized broadcaster of TV programs in Shaanxi Province approved by the Shaanxi Provincial Government, Guangdian Network currently holds a 100% share in the cable TV transmission service market within Shaanxi Province. At the same time, since the cable TV transmission service market is subject to provincial monopoly, there are significant barriers to market entry. The first-instance court considered that establishing a large-scale transmission network for cable TV transmission services requires high investment, and even without the monopoly, market entry is relatively difficult. Therefore, since Guangdian Network stated in its defense that it holds a dominant position in the cable TV transmission service market within Shaanxi Province, this court so finds in accordance with the law.

Third, whether Guangdian Network abused its dominant market position, i.e., whether Guangdian Network used its dominant position in the relevant market to engage in tying or impose other unreasonable trading conditions. The prerequisite for determining an abuse of dominant market position is whether the accused infringer holds a dominant market position. This is because the prohibition under the Antimonopoly Law on tying without justification or imposing other unreasonable trading conditions in transactions is based on the actor's possession of a dominant market position. Tying is the act of a seller, when signing a contract with a buyer, forcing the buyer to purchase products or services that, by their nature or in trading practice, are unrelated to the contract. To constitute imposing unreasonable trading conditions under the Antimonopoly Law, it must be satisfied that: conditions are attached to the transaction with the counterparty; the attached conditions require the counterparty to accept them simultaneously when conducting the transaction; the attached conditions violate the true intention of the counterparty; and there is no reasonable justification for the attached conditions. In this case, during the market transaction with Wu Xiaoqin, Guangdian Network did not inform Wu Xiaoqin that she had a choice regarding related TV program services but directly requested that Wu Xiaoqin pay the full fee including both the basic digital TV viewing maintenance fee and the digital TV pay program fee. This effectively bundled the basic digital TV viewing service and the digital TV pay program service together for sale to Wu Xiaoqin. Furthermore, by leveraging its dominant position in the cable TV transmission service market within Shaanxi Province, it compelled Wu Xiaoqin to accept the digital TV pay program service, which violated Wu Xiaoqin's will. Because of Guangdian Network's dominant market position, Wu Xiaoqin had no choice but to accept the above unreasonable conditions. Therefore, Guangdian Network's conduct constitutes the tying or imposition of other unreasonable trading conditions prohibited by the Antimonopoly Law. The defense by Guangdian Network that it did not abuse its dominant market position is inconsistent with the facts, and the court declines to accept it pursuant to law. During the trial, Guangdian Network argued that tying is the bundled sale of two products, while the program packages it offered were essentially different quantity combinations of the same product and did not constitute tying. The court noted that tying requires that the goods or services traded together are independent from each other in nature and in trading practice. When two goods or services are considered not independent of each other, such a sale cannot be deemed tying. In this case, Guangdian Network provided Wu Xiaoqin with two services: the basic viewing program service and the value-added pay program service. Watching basic viewing programs falls within the scope of basic consumption, while watching value-added pay programs falls outside the scope of basic consumption. Both appear as TV programs in form, but they are two separate and independent products that can be consumed separately, each with its own distinct demand. Therefore, the basic viewing program service and the value-added pay program service are separable products in both nature and trading practice. Consequently, this defense by Guangdian Network lacks sufficient factual basis, and the court declines to support it pursuant to law.

Finally, whether the tying or imposition of other unreasonable trading conditions by Guangdian Network had a legitimate justification. Article 8 of the Supreme People's Court's Provisions on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Disputes Arising from Monopolistic Conduct stipulates: Where the alleged monopolistic conduct falls under the abuse of dominant market position as specified in Article 17(1) of the Antimonopoly Law, the plaintiff shall bear the burden of proof regarding the defendant's dominant position in the relevant market and its abuse of that dominant position. If the defendant defends on the grounds that its conduct is legitimate, it shall bear the burden of proof. In this case, Guangdian Network did not provide any evidence regarding the legitimacy of its tying or imposition of other unreasonable trading conditions. It merely claimed that it had a responsibility to provide users with more TV programs and had the right to charge fees beyond the basic viewing programs to ensure the normal maintenance and upgrade of the network. Guangdian Network certainly may provide additional program services and charge fees beyond the basic viewing programs; however, the provision of additional program services must not violate the Antimonopoly Law. The above assertions by Guangdian Network cannot constitute a legitimate justification for its tying or imposition of other unreasonable trading conditions. Therefore, it should be held that Guangdian Network engaged in conduct constituting tying or the imposition of other unreasonable trading conditions prohibited by the Antimonopoly Law.

(2) Whether the act of Guangdian Network charging Wu Xiaoqin the digital TV pay program fee is valid

Article 15 of the Supreme People's Court's Provisions on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Disputes Arising from Monopolistic Conduct stipulates: Where the content of a contract under dispute, articles of association of an industry association, etc., violate the mandatory provisions of the Antimonopoly Law or other laws or administrative regulations, the people's court shall determine their invalidity according to law. In this case, Guangdian Network, by leveraging its dominant position in the cable TV transmission service market within Shaanxi Province, tied the provision of digital TV pay program services to the provision of basic digital TV viewing services, thereby violating the provisions of Article 17(1)(5) of the Antimonopoly Law. It is important to emphasize that the provisions of Article 17(1)(5) of the Antimonopoly Law are mandatory provisions. Pursuant to Article 52 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Contract Law), which states: "A contract shall be void under any of the following circumstances: ... (5) it violates the mandatory provisions of laws or administrative regulations," and Article 56, which states: "A void contract or a contract that has been rescinded is not legally binding ab initio. If a part of the contract is void without affecting the validity of the remaining parts, the remaining parts shall remain valid," Wu Xiaoqin's request to confirm the invalidity of the part of the digital TV service contract between her and Guangdian Network concerning the tied digital TV pay program service is supported by this court pursuant to law.

In summary, Wu Xiaoqin is a proper plaintiff in this case. Guangdian Network, by bundling the basic digital TV viewing service and the digital TV pay program service together for sale to Wu Xiaoqin, and by leveraging its dominant position in the cable TV transmission service market within Shaanxi Province to compel Wu Xiaoqin to accept the digital TV pay program service, constituted tying or the imposition of other unreasonable trading conditions, violating Article 17(1)(5) of the Antimonopoly Law of the People's Republic of China. Wu Xiaoqin's claims for a declaration that Guangdian Network's act of charging her RMB 15 for digital TV program fees is invalid and for an order to return the RMB 15 are established, and this court supports them pursuant to law. Pursuant to Article 17 and Article 50 of the Antimonopoly Law of the People's Republic of China; Articles 52, 56, and 58 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China; Articles 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, and 15 of the Supreme People's Court's Provisions on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Disputes Arising from Monopolistic Conduct; and Article 108 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the court hereby makes the following judgment: 1. It is confirmed that the act of the defendant, Shaanxi Broadcast & TV Network Intermediary (Group) Co., Ltd., in charging the plaintiff, Wu Xiaoqin, RMB 15 as a digital TV program fee on May 10, 2012, is invalid; 2. The defendant, Shaanxi Broadcast & TV Network Intermediary (Group) Co., Ltd., shall refund RMB 15 to the plaintiff, Wu Xiaoqin, within ten days from the date this judgment takes effect. If the obligation to pay monetary amount is not fulfilled within the period specified in this judgment, interest on the debt for the period of delayed performance shall be doubled in accordance with Article 229 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. The case acceptance fee of RMB 50 shall be borne by the defendant, Shaanxi Broadcast & TV Network Intermediary (Group) Co., Ltd.

Dissatisfied with the judgment, Guangdian Network filed an appeal with the Shaanxi High People's Court, requesting the following: 1. To reverse the original judgment and render a new judgment confirming that its act of charging Wu Xiaoqin RMB 15 as a digital TV program fee on May 10, 2012, is valid; 2. All litigation costs of the first and second instance to be borne by Wu Xiaoqin. Its grounds for appeal were: 1. The first-instance judgment was factually erroneous. (1) Regarding the determination of the dominant position. In Shaanxi Province, there should be at least three digital TV service providers that have a competitive relationship in the relevant market: China Telecom, China Mobile, and Guangdian Network. From this perspective alone, Guangdian Network is not the digital TV service provider possessing a dominant position as found by the first-instance court. Therefore, the first-instance court's finding that Guangdian Network had a dominant position in the relevant market based on Guangdian Network's own admission constitutes a clear error in fact-finding. (2) Regarding the determination of the illegal tying conduct. Guangdian Network's conduct conformed to the practice of tying and constituted lawful tying. The tying of digital TV pay programs by Guangdian Network was carried out with the support of national policy, not a private act. Therefore, Guangdian Network's tying conduct can be fully characterized as normal sales conduct, or even as not constituting tying at all. 2. The first-instance judgment lacked sufficient evidence for its fact-finding. Wu Xiaoqin did not provide evidence to prove that Guangdian Network had a dominant position in the relevant market; therefore, the first-instance court's finding that Guangdian Network had a dominant position in the relevant market was insufficiently supported by evidence.

In her second-instance defense, Wu Xiaoqin argued: 1. The original judgment had clearly found the facts. 2. The original judgment correctly applied the law. (1) In this case, there is no need to define the relevant market. (2) If the relevant market must be defined in this case, then digital TV constitutes a relevant product market. (3) Guangdian Network holds a dominant market position in this relevant market. (4) Guangdian Network abused its dominant market position by engaging in tying conduct regulated by the Antimonopoly Law.

After investigation in the second instance, it was found that during the first-instance trial, Guangdian Network provided copies of four specialized fee receipts, showing that around May 10, its business hall collected a monthly service fee of RMB 25. As the originals were not provided, Wu Xiaoqin declined to cross-examine them. After the trial, Guangdian Network provided the originals of three of these receipts, which were examined and cross-examined by both parties. These receipts all showed an annual payment amount of RMB 300, i.e., RMB 25 per month. In the second instance, Guangdian Network provided the originals of five receipts, including the three the originals of which had been provided in the first instance, and the transaction locations were all in Xianyang City. From this, it can be determined that around May 10, Guangdian Network provided a monthly fee service of RMB 25. The second-instance court also confirmed that the other facts of the case found by the first-instance court were true.

The second-instance court held that Article 17 of the Antimonopoly Law provides: "Business operators with a dominant market position are prohibited from engaging in the following acts of abusing their dominant market position: ... (5) tying goods without justification, or imposing other unreasonable trading conditions in transactions; ...". Wu Xiaoqin filed her first-instance lawsuit precisely based on this article. After trial, the first-instance court held that Guangdian Network's conduct met the characteristics of the prohibited act under this article and therefore ruled in favor of Wu Xiaoqin's claim. However, based on the facts found in the second instance, before and after the time Wu Xiaoqin purchased the service, Guangdian Network had also provided a basic monthly fee service of RMB 25 to unspecified persons. Therefore, it can be determined that Guangdian Network provided not only the value-added service at RMB 30 per month but also the basic service at RMB 25 per month to customers. Since there were no circumstances in this case, such as limiting the sales target, which constitute imposing other unreasonable trading conditions during the transaction, and since Wu Xiaoqin's first-instance claim was to declare that Guangdian Network's act of charging her a monthly digital TV program fee of RMB 5 was invalid for violating the Antimonopoly Law and to order the return of the corresponding fees, the key issue in this case became whether Guangdian Network's monthly fee service of RMB 30 provided to Wu Xiaoqin constituted the forbidden act under the Antimonopoly Law: a business operator with a dominant market position tying goods without justification.

The Antimonopoly Law regulates three types of monopolistic conduct: "(1) business operators reaching monopoly agreements; (2) business operators abusing dominant market positions; (3) concentrations of business operators that have or may have the effect of eliminating or restricting competition." This case concerns the second type, i.e., whether a business operator has abused its dominant market position. It should be noted that a dominant market position per se is not prohibited by law. Only when the dominant market position is abused — in this case, meaning the combination of a dominant market position with tying goods without justification — does it become conduct prohibited by the Antimonopoly Law. Therefore, examining these two aspects is the key to distinguishing between normal combined sales conduct and tying conduct prohibited by the Antimonopoly Law.

First, whether Guangdian Network had a dominant market position. Article 18 of the Antimonopoly Law provides: "The determination of whether an operator has a dominant market position shall be based on the following factors: (1) the operator's market share in the relevant market and the competitive conditions in the relevant market; (2) the operator's ability to control the sales market or the raw material procurement market; (3) the operator's financial strength and technical conditions; (4) the degree of dependence of other operators on the operator in transactions; (5) the difficulty for other operators to enter the relevant market; (6) other factors related to the determination of the operator's dominant market position." The first-instance court conducted a detailed investigation into these factors, and Guangdian Network's agent also acknowledged them during the first-instance trial. Although Guangdian Network denied this in the second instance, based on the facts found, it can be determined that in the cable TV transmission market, Guangdian Network holds advantages in various factors such as market access, market share, market position, and business scale, and thus occupies a dominant position.

Second, whether Guangdian Network's sales conduct constituted an abuse of dominant market position, i.e., whether it constituted tying without justification. Tying conduct is illegal because it hinders the order of market competition. One of the legislative purposes of regulating tying conduct is to protect the buyer's right to choose. In real life, combined sales of two or more products are not uncommon. This type of sales method may constitute tying or may be normal combined sales conduct. Simple combined sales conduct is not prohibited by law. If combined sales can enable consumers to obtain goods or services more economically than purchasing them separately, consumers may not necessarily reject such sales conduct. Only when combined sales violate the consumer's will and leave the consumer with no alternative due to the operator's dominant position does it constitute the tying conduct prohibited by the Antimonopoly Law. Distinguishing between the two requires analysis based on the characteristics of tying conduct.

Tying refers to the act of a seller requiring the counterparty to a transaction to purchase two or more goods or services together. The prerequisites for constituting tying should be: 1. There exist two or more independent products that can be sold separately in the sales conduct; 2. The seller adopts a method of not selling them separately when making the sale. The Notice on Strengthening the Administration of Cable TV Charges and Related Issues (Fagai Jiage [2009] No. 2201) jointly issued by the National Development and Reform Commission and the State Administration of Radio, Film and Television on August 25, 2009, states: "Basic cable TV viewing maintenance fees are subject to government pricing; fees for cable TV value-added business services and digital TV pay programs are to be determined independently by cable TV operating entities." This notice clarifies that the charges for basic services are set by the government, while cable TV operating entities can independently determine charges for value-added services and pay programs. It can be seen that although basic cable TV services and value-added services or pay programs are both TV programs, since they can be consumed separately, they are separable goods or services. Among them, basic services are priced by the government, while the pricing of value-added services and pay programs is determined by the operating entity independently. Admittedly, due to the product characteristics, public utility nature, and pricing methods of cable TV services, consumers generally need to purchase basic services before having the option to purchase value-added services. However, since basic services and value-added services are priced and charged separately, and in fact they correspond to different consumer demands, their separate sale does not affect their use value. Wu Xiaoqin's lawsuit did not object to the price and collection method of the government-priced basic viewing maintenance fee. Therefore, in this case, the two constitute separable products or services. The illegality of tying lies in the fact that a consumer cannot obtain the tying product without simultaneously purchasing the tied product. Coupled with the condition of a dominant market position, this means the consumer has no choice but to accept the combined sale offered by the operator, which violates the consumer's purchasing will. Moreover, it excludes competition by depriving the buyer of the freedom to choose, making it anti-competitive. Therefore, legislation prohibits it. In other words, whether the option to purchase a single product or service exists is the key factor in distinguishing tying from normal combined sales conduct. This option is not a choice between different combined sales methods, but a choice between separate sale and combined sale. In this case, Guangdian Network did not adopt a method of not selling separately when making the sale. It provided not only combined services but also basic services, meaning more than one option existed. In particular, the basic viewing maintenance fee was subject to government pricing, and in fact, separate purchase transactions existed in the same period, indicating that consumers could choose not to purchase the combined sales package. The option itself existed. Since the option existed, the constituent elements of tying conduct were not met. If tying conduct cannot be established, there is no need to further determine whether the sales conduct is the tying without justification that the Antimonopoly Law aims to regulate. Therefore, the second-instance court held that Guangdian Network's sales conduct did not constitute the tying without justification regulated by the Antimonopoly Law, and it could not be determined that the company had engaged in conduct abusing its dominant market position.

At the same time, the court also noted that the existence of an option and the method of exercising an option are two completely different legal issues. Not all conduct affecting options can be regulated by the Antimonopoly Law. If, when providing services to Wu Xiaoqin, Guangdian Network failed to truthfully inform her that a basic service option existed, leading the consumer to misjudge the consumption items and prices, this would infringe upon other rights of Wu Xiaoqin, such as her right to know, and should be protected under the Consumer Protection Law or the Contract Law, rather than being regulated by the Antimonopoly Law. This issue pertains to another legal relationship, and the burden of proof and applicable law are also different from this lawsuit, so this case will not focus on it.

In summary, Guangdian Network's sales conduct towards Wu Xiaoqin did not constitute the tying conduct prohibited by the Antimonopoly Law. Its grounds for appeal were partially established, and the appeal request is supported by the second-instance court.

Accordingly, following deliberation and decision by the Adjudication Committee of the second-instance court, and pursuant to Article 170(1)(2) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 2 of the Supreme People's Court's Provisions on Evidence in Civil Proceedings, and Article 17 of the Antimonopoly Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows: 1. The civil judgment No. (2012) Xi Min Si Chu Zi No. 00438 of the Xi'an Intermediate People's Court is reversed; 2. Wu Xiaoqin's claims are dismissed. Litigation costs for the first instance and second instance, each RMB 50, are to be borne by Wu Xiaoqin. The judgment of the second instance is final.

Upon investigation during the proceedings of this court, the facts found by the original trial court were found to be substantially true, and this court confirms them. During the proceedings of this court, Guangdian Network submitted to this court screenshots of its 2016 website fee packages, the Circular on Printing and Distributing the "Implementation Measures for Mass Business in 2016 (Trial)", and some customer fee invoices from 2016.

The Court further finds that: the civil judgment (2013) Shaan Min San Zhong Zi No. 38 of the Shaanxi High People's Court recorded that the panel members were Presiding Judge Tong Huihui, Acting Judge Song Xiaomin, Acting Judge Chang Baotang, and Clerk Zhang Huiying. The court issued a correction ruling on March 12, 2014, stating: "In the civil judgment (2013) Shaan Min San Zhong Zi No. 38 rendered by this court on September 12, 2013, in the dispute over bundling transaction between Shaanxi Broadcast & TV Network Media (Group) Co., Ltd. and Wu Xiaoqin, there were typographical errors that should be corrected. The ruling is as follows: on page 20 of the civil judgment (2013) Shaan Min San Zhong Zi No. 38, 'Acting Judge Song Xiaomin' is corrected to 'Acting Judge Feng Ju'."

Opinion of the Court

Based on the retrial applicant's reasons for retrial and the respondent's defense submissions, the issues in dispute in this case are: 1. Whether the alleged conduct in this case violates Article 17, Paragraph 1, Item 5 of the Anti-Monopoly Law; 2. Whether the court of first instance properly applied the Anti-Monopoly Law; 3. Whether there was procedural violation in the trial of the court of second instance.

1. Whether the alleged conduct in this case violates Article 17, Paragraph 1, Item 5 of the Anti-Monopoly Law

Article 17, Paragraph 1, Item 5 of the Anti-Monopoly Law prohibits a business operator with a dominant market position from, without justifiable reasons, tying in commodities or imposing other unreasonable trading conditions at the time of transaction. In this case, in its defense at first instance, Broadcast & TV Network expressly admitted that it "is a business operator approved by the Shaanxi Provincial Government to be the sole legal operator of cable television transmission services in Shaanxi Province. As the sole centralized broadcaster and controller of television programs in Shaanxi Province, Broadcast & TV Network has a dominant market position in the Shaanxi cable television market. It encourages users to select richer cable television packages, but has not abused its dominant market position, nor has it forced users to consume service items beyond basic viewing services." At second instance, although Broadcast & TV Network did not admit this, it did not present evidence to show it lacks a dominant market position. During this court's review of the retrial application, Broadcast & TV Network did not object to the fact that the courts of first and second instance found it to have a dominant market position. This court holds that, given Broadcast & TV Network is the sole legal operator of cable television transmission services in Shaanxi Province and the sole centralized broadcaster and controller of television programs in the province, the courts of first and second instance, based on the facts found, determined that Broadcast & TV Network has advantages in various elements such as market access, market share, business status, and business scale in the cable television transmission market, and occupies a dominant position; this finding is not improper.

Regarding whether Broadcast & TV Network engaged in tying when providing services to Wu Xiaoqin. Article 17, Paragraph 1, Item 5 of the Anti-Monopoly Law prohibits business operators with a dominant market position from tying in commodities without justifiable reasons. In this case, according to the facts found by the original trial court, when providing services, Broadcast & TV Network's staff informed Wu Xiaoqin that the monthly minimum charge standard had been raised from RMB 25 to RMB 30 since March 2012, and that a minimum of one quarter's payment was required each time, without informing Wu Xiaoqin that she could separately pay the basic cable television viewing maintenance fee or the digital television pay-program fee. Wu Xiaoqin, through consultation with the Broadcast & TV Network customer service center (service hotline number 96766), learned that the Broadcast & TV Network program had been upgraded, adding different pay programs with different packages, among which the minimum package basic viewing fee was RMB 360 per year, RMB 30 per month, and users should pay at least three months' fees each time. Based on the aforementioned facts, combined with the fact that the dedicated fee receipt issued by Broadcast & TV Network to Wu Xiaoqin recorded the charge items - digital television basic viewing maintenance fee of RMB 75 and digital television program fee of RMB 15, it can be determined that Broadcast & TV Network actually bundled the digital television basic viewing programs and digital television pay programs together for sale to Wu Xiaoqin, without informing Wu Xiaoqin whether she could separately select the service item of digital television basic viewing service. Furthermore, the reply from the Broadcast & TV Network customer service center (service hotline number 96766) also corroborates that when providing this service, Broadcast & TV Network charged and provided the digital television basic viewing maintenance fee and digital television pay program fee together. Although Broadcast & TV Network submitted at second instance relevant receipts showing it separately charged other users for the digital television basic viewing maintenance fee, this evidence only proves that there were exceptions to the packages described by the customer service center when collecting such fees. In the proceedings before this court, Broadcast & TV Network did not provide a reasonable explanation for the exceptions to the packages described by the customer service center, and the receipts it submitted to this court showing separate charges occurred after the litigation in this case, which is insufficient to prove the situation at the time of the lawsuit; this court does not accept this evidence. Therefore, the existence of exceptions to the packages described by the customer service center is insufficient to deny the general practice of Broadcast & TV Network charging the digital television basic viewing maintenance fee and digital television pay program fee together. The court of second instance found that Broadcast & TV Network provided not only bundled services but also basic services; the evidence was insufficient, and this court corrects that finding. Accordingly, the existing evidence cannot prove that ordinary consumers could pay only the television basic viewing maintenance fee or the digital television pay program fee, i.e., it cannot prove the existence of consumer choice. The court of second instance, without being able to prove whether a choice existed, directly considered this case as involving an issue of infringing consumer rights to information due to failure to inform consumers of a choice, and on that basis, found that Broadcast & TV Network's sales conduct did not constitute tying without justifiable reasons regulated by the Anti-Monopoly Law; the factual and legal basis was insufficient, and this court corrects that.

Based on the facts found by this court, the digital television basic viewing maintenance fee and the digital television pay program fee are two separate services. In the original trial and in this court's proceedings, Broadcast & TV Network did not prove that providing the two services together is consistent with the trade usage for providing digital television services; at the same time, if the digital television basic viewing maintenance fee and the digital television pay program fee were charged separately, there is no evidence that this would harm the performance and use value of the two services; moreover, Broadcast & TV Network did not provide justifiable reasons for the aforementioned conduct. Under these circumstances, Broadcast & TV Network, by using its dominant market position to charge the digital television basic viewing maintenance fee and digital television pay program fee together, objectively affects consumers' choice to select other service providers to provide relevant digital pay programs, and also disadvantages other service providers from entering this television service market, having an adverse effect on market competition. Therefore, the court of first instance correctly found that this violated Article 17, Paragraph 1, Item 5 of the Anti-Monopoly Law; there is no impropriety. Part of Wu Xiaoqin's reasons for retrial are established, and this court supports them.

2. Whether the court of first instance properly applied the Anti-Monopoly Law

In this lawsuit, Broadcast & TV Network argued in its defense that the occurrence of this case is essentially a dispute over whether the rights that Wu Xiaoqin should enjoy under the Consumer Protection Law were infringed, and has nothing to do with monopolistic conduct. It argued that the court of first instance should not have applied the Anti-Monopoly Law and related provisions to find that it held a dominant market position and thus ruled its charging conduct invalid. This court holds that, according to Article 226 and Article 228 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, the people's court shall, based on the parties' claims, defense submissions, and evidence exchange, summarize the issues in dispute and solicit the parties' opinions on the summarized issues. During the trial, the court shall focus on the facts, evidence, and legal application in dispute between the parties. According to the facts found by this court, Wu Xiaoqin clearly stated in her complaint that "the defendant, by charging the plaintiff a digital television program fee, actually added service content beyond the scope of the services provided, and the plaintiff should have the right to choose regarding this. The defendant is a public utility enterprise or other business operator that has a monopoly position according to law, and holds a dominant position in the digital television market. The defendant's aforementioned conduct violates Article 17, Paragraph 1, Item 5 of the Anti-Monopoly Law of the PRC, which prohibits business operators with a dominant market position from engaging in abuse of market dominance by tying commodities without justifiable reasons or imposing other unreasonable trading conditions at the time of transaction, infringing upon the plaintiff's legitimate rights and interests. Pursuant to the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Disputes Arising from Monopolistic Conduct, the plaintiff brings this civil lawsuit, requesting the court to confirm that the defendant's bundling transaction is invalid and to order the defendant to return RMB 15 to the plaintiff." In that complaint, Wu Xiaoqin did not claim that her consumer rights were harmed. Therefore, the court of first instance, based on Wu Xiaoqin's claims, properly tried the case under the Anti-Monopoly Law; there is no impropriety. This defense ground of Broadcast & TV Network cannot be established, and this court does not support it.

3. The procedural issue in this case

Wu Xiaoqin applied for retrial, arguing that when the court of second instance tried this case, it replaced panel members after the trial session, which falls under the circumstance of "illegal composition of the trial organization" as provided in Article 200, Paragraph 1, Item 7 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC. This court finds through investigation that the panel of the court of second instance consisted of judges Tong Huihui, Chang Baotang, and Feng Ju, and it was this panel that participated in the deliberation of the case. Although the judgment served to the parties recorded the panel judges as Tong Huihui, Song Xiaomin, and Chang Baotang, the court issued a correction ruling on March 12, 2014, stating: "In the civil judgment (2013) Shaan Min San Zhong Zi No. 38 rendered by this court on September 12, 2013, in the dispute over bundling transaction between Shaanxi Broadcast & TV Network Media (Group) Co., Ltd. and Wu Xiaoqin, there were typographical errors that should be corrected. The ruling is as follows: on page 20 of the civil judgment (2013) Shaan Min San Zhong Zi No. 38, 'Acting Judge Song Xiaomin' is corrected to 'Acting Judge Feng Ju'." There is no circumstance of replacing panel members after the trial session. Therefore, this ground for retrial of Wu Xiaoqin cannot be established, and this court does not support it.

In summary, Broadcast & TV Network has a dominant market position in the cable television transmission service market in Shaanxi Province. By bundling digital television basic viewing services and digital television pay program services together for sale to Wu Xiaoqin, it violated Article 17, Paragraph 1, Item (5) of the Anti-Monopoly Law of the PRC. Wu Xiaoqin's retrial claims to confirm that Broadcast & TV Network's act of charging her RMB 15 for digital television program fees is invalid and to request an order for the return of RMB 15 are established, and this court supports them. The judgment of first instance has clear fact-finding and correct application of law, and this court affirms it. The judgment of second instance has insufficient factual basis and erroneous application of law, and this court corrects it. Pursuant to Article 17, Paragraph 1, Item (5) of the Anti-Monopoly Law of the PRC and Article 200, Item (7) and Article 207 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, the judgment is as follows:

1. The civil judgment (2013) Shaan Min San Zhong Zi No. 38 of the Shaanxi High People's Court is reversed.

2. The civil judgment (2012) Xi Min Si Chu Zi No. 438 of the Xi'an Intermediate People's Court of Shaanxi Province is affirmed.

The litigation fees for first instance and second instance are each RMB 50, to be borne by Shaanxi Broadcast & TV Network Media (Group) Co., Ltd.

This judgment is final.
